reasons: Passages are as cited: Þiðreks saga, Ecca describing his gilded arms (shield with 'rautt' 'gvll'), and a late historical song about Ivan IV and Mariya Temryukovna (poisoned shirts of 'красна' 'золота'). Only one cross-branch cognate element: ON gull ~ Russ. золото (*ǵʰl̥h₃-tó- / *ǵʰolh₃-to-, ablaut variants of one root; fine). 'Red' is not cognate: красный continues Slavic *krasьnъ, whose primary sense is 'beautiful' (OCS krasьnъ 'beautiful, pleasant', Derksen), so the Russian collocation may well be 'fine gold' and the colour sense secondary; calling it a renewal of *h₁rowdʰós is special pleading. Where 'red' is cognate (ON rauðr, OE rēad, MW rhudd) the gold word is not (Welsh aur, Irish ór are Latin loans), so no branch pair shares both elements except within Germanic. 'Red gold' for high-carat gold is a natural description in many languages (generic), very frequent in byliny (197 of 1368 gold units with красн-), and the Norse anchor sits in a saga translated from Low German, where MHG 'rôt' gold is a commonplace. At most a Germanic (and NW-European) poetic idiom, not demonstrably PIE.
checked_loci: search: byliny gold units with красн- (197) / червон- (13); Germanic *h1rowdhos+gold near 3 (32 units: Laxdæla, AM 242 fol, etc.)
known: 'Red gold' is a familiar Germanic poetic epithet (rautt gull, read gold) and a byliny cliché (красное/червонное золото); no secure PIE formula to my knowledge.

reasons: Passages verified: RV 2.12.7c and 1.32.4c have Indra as subject of 'jajā́na'/'janáyan' with objects 'sū́ryam' and 'uṣásam' (1.32.4c also 'dyā́m'); also 3.32.8d and 3.31.15d (with 'agním' and 'gātúm'); Il. 5.267 'ἠῶ' and 'ἠέλιόν' in a world-merism of horses 'under dawn and sun'; Hes. Th. 371-374 Theia bore Helios, Selene and Eos ('γείναθ''). Etymologies sound: sū́rya- ~ ἥλιος (*seh₂ul-/*sóh₂wl̥), uṣás- ~ ἠώς (*h₂éwsōs), jan- ~ γείνατο (*ǵenh₁-). So there are real cognates, but the collocation is weak: sun and dawn are the two morning luminaries and co-occur in any language; Greek pairs them in a directional/merism formula and in a genealogy where Moon is the third member and a mother bears them, whereas the Vedic is a demiurge (Indra) 'generating' the light, sometimes with sky, Agni, path. The 'begot Sun and Dawn' frame is not congruent (divine maternity vs heroic creation), and the Iliad anchor is not cosmogonic at all. Defensible as a shared cosmological pair, not compelling as inherited wording.
known: Indra's begetting of Sun and Dawn is a standard RV motif; Sun and Dawn as IE divine figures (and Helios/Eos as siblings) are widely discussed in the comparative mythology literature.

reasons: Passages verified: Il. 4.235 'πατὴρ' 'Ζεὺς' as helper/guarantor against oath-breakers; AVŚ 9.10.23 'dyaur' ... 'pitā' 'janitā' with Earth as 'mātā' (= RV 1.164.33). Both elements exact cognates: Ζεύς ~ dyaúḥ (*dyḗws), πατήρ ~ pitā́ (*ph₂tḗr), nominative, the kinship title applied to the sky-god; supported by the vocative 'dyaùḥ' 'pítar' (RV 6.51.5) = Greek vocative 'Ζεῦ' 'πάτερ' and Latin Iuppiter, Umbrian Iupater. Not generic (a specific divine name + title), not derivative. Word order and pragmatic context differ (Greek oath-guarantor, Vedic cosmic parent with Earth as mother), but the fixed designation is the point. The AVŚ anchor is itself a repetition of RV 1.164.33 (intra-Indic, irrelevant to independence).
known: Yes: Dyaus pitar / Zeus pater / Iuppiter is the textbook example of an inherited PIE divine epithet (*dyēus ph₂tēr), discussed in every handbook.

reasons: Passages verified: Þiðreks saga, Fasold to Þiðrek: 'stalst' (2sg pret. mediopassive of stela, 'you stole upon', with á + acc. 'broðor') and 'sovanda' (acc. sg. pres. ptc. of sofa), followed by 'drapt'; Þiðrek replies he did not kill him 'sovanda'; AVŚ 8.6.15 'tsarati' with acc. 'tvā' 'svapantīṃ', opposed to 'jāgratīm' (demon creeping on a woman asleep or awake). Formally two cognate elements in congruent syntax (stealth verb + acc. victim + predicative pres. ptc. 'sleeping'): sofandi ~ svapant- (*swep-) secure; stela ~ tsar- (*tsel-) is Kroonen/Lubotsky 2009 (Kroonen PGm 476-477, citing reflexive stelask 'sneak' as the old sense), but LIV2 marks tsarati with '?' under *sel- and EWAia I 687 derives tsar- from *(H)d-sel-, so the equation is contested (qualification: low confidence; source LIV2 s.v. 3.*sel- and EWAia s.v. TSAR; doubt = alternative analysis as *ad-sel- compound). Generic risk: a stealthy approach naturally targets a sleeping victim; the asleep/awake contrast is a natural polar pair. Context differs (Vedic: demonic molestation of a pregnant woman; Norse: killing a warrior in his sleep), and the Norse text is a translation from Low German, though reflexive 'stelask' is native idiom. Each combination is unique in its corpus. Interesting, not compelling.
checked_loci: search: *swep- + st[ae]l- (Germanic) and tsar- (Indo-Iranian): only the two anchors

known: The stela ~ tsar- equation is Kroonen & Lubotsky 2009; I know of no discussion of this phrase as a formula.

reasons: Passages verified: Þiðreks saga, the townsmen surrendering to Attila: 'stondum' 'firir' 'yðrum' 'kníom' 'we stand before your knees' (dat. pl.), after laying down arms and coming barefoot; Hdt. 1.112.1 the herdsman's wife 'λαβομένη' 'γουνάτων' of her husband to beg for the child. Support Njáls saga 41r:14 ('kné' 'ganga' ... 'biðja' 'liðsinnis') confirms a native ON idiom 'go before someone's knees' = beg humbly. Only one cognate element: kné ~ γόνυ (*ǵónu), with the supplicated as possessor; the verbs are not cognate (stand/go vs take/grasp), and the gestures differ (Greek clasping the knees vs Norse presenting oneself at the knees/kneeling). Kneeling or falling at the knees of a superior is a near-universal submission gesture and also biblical/Latin ad genua; the Norse anchor is in a translation from Low German. The Njáls idiom makes a native Germanic usage plausible, so the parallel is defensible but generic.

known: Knee-supplication (γούνων λαβέσθαι) is well studied in Greek; the knee in IE supplication/kinship is discussed in the literature (e.g. Onians, Benveniste); not to my knowledge with this ON idiom.

reasons: Passages verified: Magnus Lagabøtir's Landslov (1274), Mannhelgi: if a man 'drepr' his 'fǫður', 'bróður', 'móður', 'dóttur' or 'systur' he is 'óbótamaðr'; AVP 19.46.26 'mātṛhā' 'pitṛhā' 'svasṛhā' among the 'duṣkṛtaḥ' (with 'bhrūṇaghnām' in 46.28). Kin terms are cognate (*ph₂tḗr, *méh₂tēr, *swésōr) but the slaying element is not in the Norse anchor (drepa); the Vedic compounds in -hán- vs a Norse conditional legal clause are not the same construction. The claimed 'same order (father/mother/sister)' is false: Vedic has mother-father-sister, Norse father-brother-mother-daughter-sister. A list of the closest kin as objects of 'kill' is generic in any moral or legal code, and the Norse royal law is heavily shaped by canon-law and Christian penitential categories (óbótamál, parricide as unemendable crime), so derivative influence is likely. The compound type *ph₂tr-gʷʰen- (pitṛhán-, πατροφόνος) is a separate comparison, and even there the Norse leg is doubtful: Kroonen (PGm s.v. *banjō-, p0089) derives ON bani < *banan- < *bʰon-on- and rejects *gʷʰ > b (against Seebold 1967), so the claim's 'bani < *gʷʰon-' is contested (qualification: low confidence; source Kroonen 2013 s.v. *banjō-; doubt = no regular *gʷʰ > Gmc *b). These anchors do not instantiate the compound type anyway.
known: Kin-slayer compounds with *gʷʰen- (pitṛhán-, πατροφόντης/πατροφονεύς, ON -bani) are noted in the literature on *gʷʰen- (e.g. Watkins, How to Kill a Dragon); the Norse law list is not.
